title: Slices With Product Under a Cap
statement:
You get an array nums of positive integers and a number k. Count the contiguous, non-empty slices of nums whose product is strictly less than k.

Slices at different positions count separately, even if they hold the same values.

examples.why: The four single values, plus [2, 5] = 10 and [5, 3] = 15. [3, 10] and [2, 5, 3] both reach exactly 30, which is not under the cap.
Every product is 1, and 1 is not strictly less than 1.
Every slice except the whole array (product 16). The 1s let a window stretch past a value without growing the product.

hints: Fix the right end of a slice. As you move its left end further left, can the product ever go down?
All values are positive, so stretching a slice never lowers its product. For each right end, the valid left ends form one unbroken range ending at the right end.

Keep a window [left, right] whose product is under k. Add nums[right]; while the product is k or more, divide out nums[left] and move left. Then every slice ending at right and starting in the window counts: right − left + 1 of them.

explain.intuition:
Positive numbers make the product grow (or stay the same) as a slice gets longer. So if a slice ending at right is under the cap, every shorter slice ending at right is too. That means the good slices ending at right are exactly those starting between some left and right: right − left + 1 of them.

When right moves one step, the smallest valid left can only move right as well, since the product just gained a factor. That is a sliding window: multiply in the new value, divide out values from the left until the product is under k again, and add the window length to the count.
steps: If k ≤ 1, return 0: every product is at least 1.
While prod ≥ k, divide by nums[left] and increase left.
Add right − left + 1 to count. Return count at the end.
pitfalls: Missing the k ≤ 1 case. With k = 1 the shrink loop empties the window and keeps going past right unless it is guarded.
Counting 1 per valid window instead of right − left + 1. Each step adds every slice that ends at right.
Using ≤ k instead of < k. In the first example that wrongly adds [3, 10] and [2, 5, 3].

solutions.title: Extend from every start
solutions.idea: For each start, multiply rightwards and stop once the product reaches k.

solutions.title: Sliding window
solutions.idea: Keep the longest window ending at right with product under k; it contributes its length to the count.

followups: Count slices whose sum is under k instead, with positive values. What stays the same?
The values may be 0 or negative. Why does the window break, and what would you use instead?
